summary:
Galaxy Match solves the "analog bottleneck" by helping mission teams instantly find the right place on Earth to rehearse planetary exploration. We built an automated engine that compares spatial targets (like Jezero Crater or Deuteronilus Mensae) against numerous Earth sites (mostly in Bolivia’s Altiplano) using open NASA and USGS data. The app scores sites across multiple dimensions (slope, roughness, temperature, etc.) using the exact same radius and resolution.

Crucially, it doesn't just rank them; it explains where the analogy fails. For example, it matches Martian plateaus topographically while noting the lack of subsurface ice. Features include a 3D terrain comparison, Perseverance’s real route replayed on Earth, and an extensive grid of measured points proposing new candidate sites. Bolivia is our pilot, proving that analog selection can be fast, transparent, and reproducible for any region.
details:
WHAT IT DOES Galaxy Match answers one critical question: which place on Earth is best for studying a phenomenon or rehearsing a task for Mars or the Moon, and what data supports that choice? The user picks a purpose (e.g., rover mobility, ancient lakes) or specific targets. The app ranks a curated catalog of Earth sites on an interactive 3D globe, showing overall similarity, dimensional scores, and plain-language notes on where the analogy fails so scientists know how to adapt their tests.

HOW IT WORKS & SCIENTIFIC RIGOR We automated the comparison by extracting numerical values from spatial data:

  • Slope and roughness come from elevation models at the exact same spatial step on every body (Terrain Tiles for Earth, USGS HRSC-MOLA for Mars, LOLA for the Moon).
  • Climate data comes from NASA POWER and the Mars Climate Database.
  • Geological settings are parsed via Macrostrat.

We applied strict scientific boundaries. For instance, when searching for an analog for Deuteronilus Mensae (Mars), our engine successfully identified Bolivia's Desierto de Siloli as a top candidate, revealing a 98.4% match in median slope (1.38° on Mars vs. 1.82° on Earth). At the same time, the app explicitly flags where the analogy fails—such as differences in wind erosion dynamics under a dense atmosphere—ensuring researchers understand the precise limits of the test site.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

TOOLS USED Web app: React 19, TypeScript, Vite, MapLibre GL JS (for 3D terrain), hosted on Vercel. Data pipeline: Python scripts to extract values from NASA/USGS rasters and build composite indicators.

CREATIVITY Mars and the Moon are treated simply as another row of data, making the method universal. We don't just show numbers; users can drag a curtain to compare Earth and Mars terrain in 3D, and even replay the Perseverance rover's exact Martian route overlaid on Bolivian soil.
